sources.news_title: Senate passes college sports bill that would rein in athlete payments,transfers
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill Monday that would regulate college sports, an attempt to end "chaos" in an industry that has been upended by skyrocketing athlete payments and near-unrestricted transfers between schools.
The overwhelming 77-22 vote to pass the legislation is the strongest effort yet by Congress to set national regulations governing payments to college athletes for their name, image and likeness and how often they can transfer. It would give the NCAA new authority over those rules and limited antitrust protections to enforce them.
The bill is the product of years of Senate negotiations that intensified after a 2025 lawsuit settlement uprooted the college sports landscape by allowing colleges to pay their players. The legislation, which would still have to pass the House, would codify the settlement into law but also establish new guardrails around the system in an attempt to rein in the runaway costs for colleges.
"It would be nice if college sports could somehow magically fix itself, but this is a matter of law, federal law, and only Congress can fix it," said Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who negotiated the bill with the top Democrat on the panel, Washington Sen. Maria Cantwell.
President Donald Trump praised the bill in a social media post after the late night passage. "This is a really big deal," he said. "It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves."
The bill's backers — more than 70 senators from both parties — say it aims to curtail constant litigation and uncertainty across college sports for athletes, schools and fans. It would also give hundreds of thousands of athletes new health and labor protections.
But critics say the bill doesn't do enough to protect athletes or curtail the enormous sums of money flowing to coaches, colleges and conferences.
"This is a bill that essentially ensconces a system of exploitation, and it doesn't fix the broader problems," said Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy, a Democrat who has worked with labor and civil rights groups to rally opposition to the bill.
The bill's future is still unclear. It could face an uphill battle in the House, which failed repeatedly over the last year to get a different version to the floor and is in recess until after the November elections.
Lawmakers will have to start over in the next Congress if the bill doesn't pass both chambers by the end of the year.
College sports have been reeling in the wake of the 2025 court settlement allowing colleges to directly pay players for their name, image and likeness. The fallout has reshaped the industry and led to football roster payrolls that can exceed $40 million.
The bill would codify the court settlement, including a revenue cap that allows schools to share up to $21.5 million in revenue with their players. The legislation would more than double that amount for some schools, allowing up to an additional $27.5 million in payments through a retention fund — a change that helped win the support of the two largest conferences, the Big Ten and Southeastern Conference.
To help schools raise more revenue, the bill would give schools and conferences the option of pooling their TV media rights.
The legislation also aims to stabilize the NCAA transfer portal that has led to players constantly switching teams. It would restrict player transfers to one "free" move over five years without sitting out a year, with some exceptions, and also would restrict players to five years of total eligibility.
The proposed eligibility limit comes amid backlash to schools that have increasingly pushed boundaries, including LSU's now-canceled plans to place players on the roster who had participated in NFL training camps.
"That was probably like a big lamp for some people who saw it and said, 'Oh my God, this is so out of control,'" Cantwell said in a recent interview with The Associated Press.
The bill also would restrict coaches from leaving their schools during the season, force schools that want to switch conferences to spend three years as an independent and prevent conferences from growing larger than 20 programs — an effort to prevent so-called "superleagues" from taking over sports. A last-minute amendment proposed by Florida Sen. Ashley Moody raised that cap from 19 in the original legislation.
The vote was delayed several hours on Monday as senators negotiated Moody's amendment and others that were eventually adopted, including a provision to make it easier for athletes to sue over sexual assault and a requirement to disclose foreign financing.
The Senate rejected an amendment by Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., that would have put limits on ticket prices for fans and two by Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., that would have capped coaches' salaries at $5 million a year and increased compensation for athletes who have catastrophic injuries.
The legislation includes new protections for athletes, including caps on agent fees and guarantees for health insurance and scholarships. It would also require schools to maintain a minimum number of sports and roster spots — an effort to ensure that women's and Olympic sports are not cut in favor of football, basketball and other sports that generate more revenue.
Still, some Democrats say it wouldn't do enough to limit the big money in college sports.
The legislation "places a cap on the students' cut of the revenues, but there are no caps on coaches' salaries or on the size of donations to athletic programs," Murphy said last week.
Groups like the NAACP, Congressional Black Caucus and AFL-CIO have also opposed the bill, in part, because it leaves unresolved whether athletes should be considered employees with the ability to collectively bargain.
All four Black Democrats in the Senate — Booker, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland — have opposed the bill.
Booker, who played football at Stanford in the late 1980s on a scholarship, noted the "outsized role" that Black athletes play in college sports. He said it wasn't until college athletes were able to begin to win cases in court that the power started to shift, "and now the NCAA is coming here to the United States Senate, asking for sweeping powers" to exempt antitrust laws.
"We know who this bill is protecting," Booker said.
Despite strong bipartisan support in the Senate, the bill faces a murky path in the House.
House lawmakers won't return to Washington until mid-November, after the elections. And it's unclear what will be on Republican leaders' agenda in the chaotic last few weeks of the session.
Pressure from Trump could help push the bill to passage. But some House Republicans have insisted on language explicitly stating that athletes are not employees, which the Senate bill does not have — a key concession to Cantwell to win enough Democratic support.
After the bill's passage, Cruz said it is his hope "that we see in the House the same thing we saw in the Senate: a big bipartisan vote."

sources.news_title: Senate passes Protect College Sports Act 77-22 for college NIL rules
sources.text:
Senate passed a sweeping college sports NIL bill 77-22, but the House is divided
The bill would codify NIL rights, cap agent fees, and give the NCAA a limited antitrust exemption, but the House is on recess and the Congressional Black Caucus opposes it
The U.S. Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act on Monday by a bipartisan vote of 77-22, setting a national framework for name, image, and likeness compensation in college sports and sending the legislation to the House of Representatives. The bill was introduced in June by Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, and Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, Democrat of Washington.
Under the legislation, athletes would have a federally protected right to earn NIL compensation, superseding the inconsistent state-by-state rules currently in place. It would also cap agent fees at 5%, limit athletes to one transfer without losing eligibility, establish a five-year eligibility cap, and require Division I schools to cover medical costs for athletic injuries for current athletes and for five years after their eligibility ends, according to Cantwell's office. The bill would also grant the NCAA and conferences a limited antitrust exemption to enforce certain rules, and allow conferences to negotiate television rights collectively.
President Donald Trump celebrated Senate passage on Truth Social, writing that the bill is "a really big deal" and that it "will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves."

U.S. Senate passes Ted Cruz’s college sports bill that seeks to rein in NCAA “chaos”
By Will Hammann and Gabby Birenbaum, The Texas Tribune 
September 28, 2026
WASHINGTON — After several months in limbo, U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz’s bill that would impose a sweeping set of regulations on college sports passed the Senate late Monday night with more than three quarters of the body’s support, marking the legislation’s furthest milestone yet.
Sponsored by Cruz, the Senate Commerce Committee chair, and Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, D-Washington, the Protect College Sports Act had remained stalled since it advanced through the committee in June. After hours of discussion Monday on amendments that saw minor changes to the bill, it finally passed in the upper chamber 77-22. The bill must still clear the U.S. House, which is in recess until after the November elections, before reaching the desk of President Donald Trump.
Cruz’s bill would install a slew of regulations to rectify what he frequently has called the “chaos” that’s emerged since the NCAA’s 2021 decision to allow college athletes to profit off their name, image and likeness, or NIL, and after a subsequent settlement a few years later, House v. NCAA, forced the association and its athletic conferences to share revenue with athletes. College athletics continue to operate under varying state laws, court rulings and NCAA regulations that govern everything from athlete compensation to conference realignment.
On the Senate floor Monday, Cruz said the bill “protects our student-athletes.”
“It protects NIL opportunities, because student-athletes deserve the opportunity to benefit from their talent without being taken advantage of by unscrupulous agents and backdoor deals,” Cruz said. “It creates clear, enforceable rules for eligibility and transfers. It protects our traditions and rivalries. It prevents the most powerful and wealthy conferences from breaking away to form a super league.”
The bill garnered fresh momentum at the start of August, when Cruz, other lawmakers and White House officials won the support of Big Ten and Southeastern Conference leaders, who got on board after Cruz and Cantwell revised the bill’s revenue sharing framework. Soon after, the White House formally voiced its support for the bill, with Trump calling on lawmakers to move quickly to pass it. Cruz has recently pressed the House to return to Capitol Hill to pass the legislation.
“What I would like to see is the speaker call the House back to pass this bill and put it on the president’s desk,” he said on his podcast last week, adding that he has “urged the president to sign it on the set of College Gameday, do it on a big game and do it going into the election.”
Among other provisions, the bill would enshrine some recent legal victories for athletes while also establishing stricter regulations on their activity. Schools and athletic organizations could no longer restrict athletes from entering NIL agreements, while athletes would have to report their revenue above $600 to their institutions. It would also limit athletes to one transfer throughout their college careers and establish permanent ceilings on their revenue, with annual adjustments for inflation.
The legislation also aims to protect athletic programs that don’t return huge profits. Division I conferences would be prohibited from reducing their schools’ required number of varsity or Olympic sports teams. Schools that make $80 million or more in annual athletics revenue would have to at least maintain 2024-25 levels of scholarships and roster spots for sports that don’t generate a profit.
For Ruben Rojas Betanzos, a Syracuse University student-athlete, president of Syracuse’s Student-Athlete Advisory Committee and vice chair of the Atlantic Coast Conference’s committee, the rapidly changing landscape has made it increasingly difficult for athletes to know what rules apply to them.
“Rules are changing so quickly that it’s almost impossible for someone to keep up,” Betanzos told The Texas Tribune. “A student-athlete in one state could be having a completely different experience from an athlete in another state.”
Betanzos, who is in his fifth year at Syracuse and completing a masters in business administration after studying bioengineering as an undergraduate, said he supports the bill’s provisions addressing healthcare, Olympic and women’s sports, and capping agent endorsement fees at 5%.
Other notable college sports figures have voiced their support for the legislation, like former University of Alabama football head coach Nick Saban and Deion Sanders, current head coach of the University of Colorado Boulder football team.
But the bill has drawn significant opposition from labor and civil rights organizations, as well as some lawmakers who argue that it would give the NCAA and athletic conferences too much control over athletes.
In an August letter to Senate leadership, NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson urged lawmakers to reject the legislation.
“Congress should not grant new federal benefits, legal protections, or economic advantages to public institutions and athletic conferences that profit from the talent and labor of Black college athletes while remaining silent as their states dilute Black voting power,” he wrote. “That arrangement is a modern version of Jim Crow.”
Black athletes make up about 20 percent of Division I athletes and more than 40 percent of Division I men’s basketball and football players, according to NCAA figures.
The AFL-CIO, a major federation of U.S. labor unions, also urged senators to oppose the bill in a letter signed by Jody Calemine, director of government affairs. The letter took aim at the legislation’s antitrust exemption for universities and conferences, and argued that the bill halts the progress that athletes have made in combating their exploitation through collusion.
“The bill only gained its current momentum not when athletes’ interests were satisfied but when the richest intercollegiate conferences in the country voted to endorse the bill,” the letter read. “That should tell you everything you need to know about who this bill protects.”
Gabby Birenbaum contributed to this report.
This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

sources.news_title: Senate resoundingly approves sweeping college sports measure
sources.text:
Senate resoundingly approves sweeping college sports measure
WASHINGTON — The Senate on Monday approved a sweeping remake of collegiate sports regulations in an effort to restore stability to an athletic landscape that has been upended by constant transfers, frequent shifts in conference membership and an infusion of money from wealthy boosters eager to lure top talent.
Known as the Protect College Sports Act, the bill passed by an overwhelming bipartisan vote of 77-22, making it one of the last major pieces of business to be tackled by lawmakers before the midterm elections. It was a bid by Congress to lay out significant new rules and standards governing popular college sports that are a mainstay of American life as well as a path to an education for student athletes.
Authors of the legislation, which faces an uncertain future in the House, said aggressive congressional intervention was necessary because a series of legal rulings had sowed chaos in college sports. They warned that the current financial path of colleges and universities was unsustainable, would decrease competition and could cause schools to jettison less popular sports that were not as lucrative as football.
“It would be nice if college sports could somehow magically fix itself, but this is a matter of law, federal law, and it is only Congress that can fix it,” said S. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, a chief proponent of the bill.
But it has run into fierce opposition from Black lawmakers and others who say the measure restricts opportunities for players, many of them Black, while doing little to hold down the pay or mobility of top coaches.
The legislation would limit college athletes to one transfer before they would have to sit out a season, as they had in the past before court rulings opened the transfer “portal,” spurring thousands of athletes to try to change schools each year. It also would set eligibility at five years. It would protect the right of college athletes to receive compensation for their “name, image and likeness” and institute guarantees for scholarships and healthcare.
The measure also would grant the NCAA, the governing body of college sports, a limited antitrust exemption while remaining silent on collective bargaining by student athletes. It attempts to discourage schools from jumping from conference to conference and it imposes new restrictions on agents for athletes.
“Sports is about any given Saturday,” said Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, the lead Democratic sponsor of the bill. “It is not about whether you have a billionaire in your backyard. It is about whether you can coach and recruit and develop and maintain and have academic performance and have fairness.”
Despite the Senate approval, opponents blasted the measure as unfair to players. An amendment to cap coaching salaries at $5 million and limit their contract buyouts to one year’s salary was defeated Monday as the authors beat back a series of proposed changes. Democratic opponents also were unhappy with the lack of clarity about future collective bargaining.
“It’s a bill for the control and power of the NCAA and member institutions,” said Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., and a top opponent of the legislation. “It is not about athletes who are winning their rights, winning court cases, gaining leverage, and now are having that taken away from them.”
But resistance to the bill was no match for the major sports conferences, state schools, big-name coaches and other powerful interest groups that got behind it, including airing television spots that featured high-profile figures such as Deion Sanders, the former professional sports star who is now the head football coach at the University of Colorado.
“The colleges and the conferences and the boosters flooded this place,” said Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., another leading opponent of the bill. “It is a hard slog when the players have no money and no representation. Ultimately, this is going to be really bad for student athletes and destructive of the college sports model because these kids aren’t going to stick around very long if they are not getting paid what they are worth.”
Others said Congress should have stayed out of the fight.
“The people who oversee the post office now want to run college sports. What could go wrong?” said Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky.
He said he doubted that the founding fathers ever envisioned that “Congress would one day be in charge of dictating the rules for college sports.”
With the House scheduled to be in recess until after the midterm elections, there is at present no clear path for the legislation to pass before Congress reconvenes in mid-November. Whether Republican leaders would take it up after the elections is unclear. Lame-duck agendas can be notoriously tricky. But President Donald Trump is an enthusiastic supporter of the legislation and could put pressure on the House to act.
“This is a really big deal,” Trump posted on social media after the vote. “It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves.”
The measure is strongly opposed by members of the Congressional Black Caucus. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the minority leader who is in line to become speaker if Democrats win the House, has repeatedly expressed reservations. He called the legislation a “work in progress.”
“I share many of the concerns that have been articulated by both the Congressional Black Caucus and the NAACP,” Jeffries said.
Those groups contend that by limiting transfers and capping the overall amount of compensation paid to athletes, the proposal shifts the balance of power back to the schools and coaches after athletes won new rights through the courts. On the other side of the issue, some House Republicans favor explicitly declaring that student athletes are not school employees, limiting their bargaining capacity.
“They have problems on both the left and the right in the House of Representatives,” Murphy said. “We are going to continue to fight this bill.”
Following the vote, Cruz said he believed the resounding approval should persuade the House Republican leadership to call the House back from recess, pass the bill and send it to the president for a signing ceremony, which he said he hoped would take place on a televised college football pregame show.
“From the beginning, our objective was not to squeak by with 60 or 61 votes but to have a big bipartisan vote that demonstrates the importance of stepping in and saving and preserving college sports,” Cruz said. “For every one of the members of the House who are out campaigning right now, it is hard to think of a more productive use of their time than coming back and passing landmark legislation on a topic that matters dearly to millions of Americans.”

The best way to understand what happened yesterday evening on the Senate floor, where the Protect College Sports Act overwhelmingly passed by a vote of 77 to 22, is that Congress responded to the college sports establishment’s plea to save it from itself. Not that anyone put it that way, of course. The bill’s lead sponsor, Ted Cruz, insisted last week that the Protect College Sports Act will “bring order to the chaos consuming the new era of college sports.” My reading of the bill, however, is that it will deprive a distinct group of Americans—college athletes—of the economic rights that every other citizen is entitled to in a country that claims to believe in capitalism.
Is there chaos in college sports? I can’t deny it. Ever since the Supreme Court concluded in 2021 that long-standing NCAA rules preventing college athletes from being paid violated the nation’s antitrust laws, an absolute gusher of money has poured into college sports. At the big-time sports schools, “collectives” of wealthy boosters are handing out millions to athletes under the guise of payments for their “name, image, and likeness” (NIL). Ohio State University, for instance, paid its football team between $49 million and $55 million this season, with star wide receiver Jeremiah Smith receiving an estimated $5 million. When you throw in what the school and its boosters pay its basketball players, its soccer players, its tennis players, and so on, it probably approaches $80 million. A similar story can be told at Louisiana State University, University of Michigan, Indiana University, and most of the other schools that get the College GameDay treatment from ESPN during football season.

sources.news_title: US Senate approves Protect College Sports Act. See how Louisiana senators voted, what’s next.
sources.text:
WASHINGTON – Legislation that pays college athletes and protects universities from most litigation headed Tuesday to the U.S. House, where it faces an uncertain future despite overwhelming support in the Senate.
Senators, who had flown into town Monday afternoon, voted late that night, 77-22, to send the Protect College Sports Act of 2026 to the House.
Both Louisiana senators, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-Baton Rouge, and Sen. John Kennedy, R-Madisonville, voted in favor of final passage.
“College sports is in desperate need for stability. This legislation sets student-athletes up for success,” Cassidy said.
“We’ve made a lot of people happy with this bill,” Kennedy said.
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, of Connecticut and a leader of the opposition, noted that LSU President Wade Rousse last week said the university’s athletic department is projected to be $26 million short this fiscal year and LSU athletics has overspent its budget over the past six years by a total of $177.5 million.
“LSU just paid a buyout of over $53 million to the coach they fired. In fact, last year the buyout for just three coaches at LSU totaled over $169 million,” Murphy said. “Yet, this bill only restricts, only caps the money going to players. Does nothing to cap the money going to coaches.”
The sweeping bill sets up a national system through which student-athletes can profit from the sale of their “name, image and likeness” and collect a portion of the revenues their games create; limits athletes’ ability to transfer between schools; and exempts universities from antitrust laws that are the avenues for lawsuits that have changed the traditional way of college sports, in which the student-athletes aren’t paid but bring in billions of dollars.
Though the legislation is in their court now, the lower chamber isn’t scheduled to return to Capitol Hill until November 9 – after voters in the congressional midterms have selected a new Congress.
When the House does return, representatives face this bill plus a full plate of work and only 20 days to do it. If the House doesn’t pass the bill and put it on Trump’s desk to sign into law, the new 120th Congress, which convenes in January, will have to start all over again.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Benton, is off campaigning in hopes of keeping the Republican majority necessary for him to stay head of the chamber. Before leaving on his cross-country trek, Johnson said passing the legislation is going to require persuading a handful of House Republicans.
The margins in the 435-seat House are so narrow that the bill is lost if all Democrats vote no and two Republicans bolt, depending on how many representatives show up.
The legislation has wide support, including from the SEC, Big 10 and other major athletic conferences, as well as coaches and President Donald Trump.
Former LSU football coach Nick Saban, who also coached at Alabama, testified before Congress over the summer that college sports need national rules, rather than allowing each state make its own.
“Without that legal certainty, every rule becomes another lawsuit, every standard becomes another risk, and the system keeps drifting toward a professional model,” Saban said.
But the bill also has significant opposition, including the NAACP, the AFL-CIO and the Congressional Black Caucus, which argue that student-athletes don’t have rights to collective bargaining under the bill and are receiving about 20% of the revenues they help create, whereas professional athletes receive about half the revenues.
Since July 2025, some House Republicans also have tried to persuade enough of their GOP colleagues, so far unsuccessfully, to back the Student Compensation and Opportunity through Rights and Endorsements Act. SCORE gives the universities more say-so than the Protect College Sports Act but otherwise is similar.
A final vote in the Senate was slowed Monday night by last-minute negotiations.
Republicans and Democrats each had four amendments they wanted attached to the instrument.
Kennedy wanted an amendment to cap ticket price increases at 4% annually.
Kennedy argued on the Senate floor that, if Congress is providing special protections to college athletics, it should also provide protections to the fans who make college sports possible.
“Everybody makes money from college sports — the universities, the coaches and the athletes. But who makes all of that possible? The fans,” Kennedy said. “My amendment would have done something for the people who pay for the tickets and make games possible by ensuring they don’t get hit with unlimited ticket-price increases.”
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, opposed Kennedy’s proposed change in wording, arguing that it amounted to setting price controls on college sporting events.
“All this bill does is fix prices,” Kennedy responded.
Cassidy also voted against Kennedy’s amendment. “I’m a conservative. I don’t think the federal government should be intervening in a private market that way,” Cassidy said.
The amendment came 18 votes shy of the 60 needed to be added to the bill.
The legislation, if enacted into law, would exempt college sports from antitrust laws, which would allow the universities to coordinate between themselves when negotiating, say, television rights. But the antitrust exemption also protects universities and their athletic departments, as well as the NCAA governing body, from most litigation.
The Protect College Sports Act roughly doubles the $21.5 million revenue sharing cap and allows the schools an additional $27 million to keep its athletes from moving to another institution; sets up an enforceable system for student-athletes to make money from the use of their name, image, and likeness; and limits agent fees. Athletes would be allowed to transfer once without having to sit out, and guarantees would allow them to use their scholarships to return to school and complete their degrees. Coaches would not be allowed to change programs during the season.

“It protects NIL opportunities, because student-athletes deserve the opportunity to benefit from their talent without being taken advantage of by unscrupulous agents and backdoor deals,” Cruz said. “It creates clear, enforceable rules for eligibility and transfers. It protects our traditions and rivalries. It prevents the most powerful and wealthy conferences from breaking away to form a super league.”
The bill garnered fresh momentum at the start of August, when Cruz, other lawmakers and White House officials won the support of Big Ten and Southeastern Conference leaders, who got on board after Cruz and Cantwell revised the bill’s revenue sharing framework. Soon after, the White House formally voiced its support for the bill, with Trump calling on lawmakers to move quickly to pass it. Cruz has recently pressed the House to return to Capitol Hill to pass the legislation.
“What I would like to see is the speaker call the House back to pass this bill and put it on the president’s desk,” he said on his podcast last week, adding that he has “urged the president to sign it on the set of College Gameday, do it on a big game and do it going into the election.”
Among other provisions, the bill would enshrine some recent legal victories for athletes while also establishing stricter regulations on their activity. Schools and athletic organizations could no longer restrict athletes from entering NIL agreements, while athletes would have to report their revenue above $600 to their institutions. It would also limit athletes to one transfer throughout their college careers and establish permanent ceilings on their revenue, with annual adjustments for inflation.
The legislation also aims to protect athletic programs that don’t return huge profits. Division I conferences would be prohibited from reducing their schools’ required number of varsity or Olympic sports teams. Schools that make $80 million or more in annual athletics revenue would have to at least maintain 2024-25 levels of scholarships and roster spots for sports that don’t generate a profit.
For Ruben Rojas Betanzos, a Syracuse University student-athlete, president of Syracuse’s Student-Athlete Advisory Committee and vice chair of the Atlantic Coast Conference’s committee, the rapidly changing landscape has made it increasingly difficult for athletes to know what rules apply to them.
“Rules are changing so quickly that it’s almost impossible for someone to keep up,” Betanzos told The Texas Tribune. “A student-athlete in one state could be having a completely different experience from an athlete in another state.”
Betanzos, who is in his fifth year at Syracuse and completing a masters in business administration after studying bioengineering as an undergraduate, said he supports the bill’s provisions addressing healthcare, Olympic and women’s sports, and capping agent endorsement fees at 5%.
Other notable college sports figures have voiced their support for the legislation, like former University of Alabama head football coach Nick Saban and University of Colorado head football coach Deion Sanders.
But the bill has drawn significant opposition from labor and civil rights organizations, as well as some lawmakers who argue that it would give the NCAA and athletic conferences too much control over athletes.
In an August letter to Senate leadership, NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson urged lawmakers to reject the legislation.
“Congress should not grant new federal benefits, legal protections, or economic advantages to public institutions and athletic conferences that profit from the talent and labor of black college athletes while remaining silent as their states dilute black voting power,” he wrote. “That arrangement is a modern version of Jim Crow.”
Black athletes make up about 20 percent of Division I athletes and more than 40 percent of Division I men’s basketball and football players, according to NCAA figures.
The AFL-CIO, a major federation of U.S. labor unions, also urged senators to oppose the bill in a letter signed by Jody Calemine, director of government affairs. The letter took aim at the legislation’s antitrust exemption for universities and conferences, and argued that the bill halts the progress that athletes have made in combating their exploitation through collusion.
“The bill only gained its current momentum not when athletes’ interests were satisfied but when the richest intercollegiate conferences in the country voted to endorse the bill,” the letter read. “That should tell you everything you need to know about who this bill protects.”

sources.news_title: Senate passes 77-22 college sports bill granting NCAA antitrust protection and federal NIL rules
sources.text:
The Senate on Monday night passed the Protect College Sports Act, a bill that would establish federal rules for name, image and likeness deals and grant the NCAA and its member conferences a limited antitrust exemption to enforce them. The final vote was 77-22.
Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the top Republican and Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, led the bill. It now moves to the House, where its fate is uncertain.
President Donald Trump had pushed lawmakers to act before the summer recess. Speaking at a White House event with Team USA athletes, he said, "I'm urging the House and the Senate to come together, bipartisan if possible and it looks like they have done, to send the bill to my desk and I will sign it."
Trump added, "I think we have no choice. We have to get that done. If we don't, we're very foolish. Nobody knows what will happen. We're in Never-Never Land. We're not going to let that be happening."
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said before the vote, "I think most people acknowledge that the current landscape of college sports is a mess. It needs to be addressed."
The Washington Examiner reports the legislation would establish a federal framework for NIL payments, cap the amount universities can give directly to athletes, create rules for transfers, and set other regulations governing college sports. According to CNN, the bill is a major overhaul of college athletics. OutKick notes it covers standards for NIL deals, athlete compensation, recruiting, eligibility and transferring.
The bill's central feature is an antitrust exemption that would allow the NCAA, conferences and schools to enforce certain rules without the threat of lawsuits that have reshaped the sport over the past several years. Court decisions dismantled the NCAA's old amateurism model and opened the door to NIL deals, which grew quickly with little national oversight.
Under the measure, the NCAA would receive greater legal protection to enforce the uniform framework, while athletes would gain a defined set of rules for compensation, transfers and eligibility.
Critics of the bill argue that capping payments could limit what athletes earn, while supporters say the current system is unsustainable. The bill passed with broad bipartisan support, drawing 77 votes in favor.
The House must now take up the legislation. If it passes there, it would go to Trump's desk. Trump has already signaled he would sign it. "I think we have no choice," he said. "We have to get that done."
Our Take
There's a reason this bill cruised through the Senate with 77 votes: college sports is broken. The courts blew up the old rules, the NCAA threw up its hands, and what followed was a free-for-all. Boosters with deep pockets bought rosters. The transfer portal turned into free agency with no salary cap. Nobody knew what was allowed, and the athletes caught in the middle had no stable framework to rely on.
Is this bill perfect? No. Washington rarely produces perfect. The antitrust exemption is the part to watch closest. Once you hand the NCAA legal cover, you have to make sure it doesn't become a license to trample the rights of the very athletes it claims to protect. The cap on direct university payments also raises a real question: who decides what a player's name and image are worth? If the answer is a bureaucrat in a conference office, that's a problem.
But this is a step toward order. And it shows that when Congress actually does its job, it can still find common ground. Trump pushed for it. Cruz and Cantwell hashed it out. The House should take it up without delay and send it to the president's desk.
If they don't, the chaos continues. Which side will your representative choose?

sources.news_title: Protect College Sports Act gains Senate approval in bipartisan vote
sources.text:
By Field Level Media
Sep 29 (Field Level Media) – The Protect College Sports Act took its next step forward on Monday, with the Senate voting overwhelmingly 77-22 in favor of the proposed federal legislation reforming college athletics.
The bipartisan bill, written by U.S. Senators Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and introduced in June, will now move on to the House of Representatives. The next scheduled House legislative session begins Nov. 9.
“There are several things in this bill that are really important to enshrine into federal law at this time. First and foremost, the federal right to NIL (Name, Image, and Likeness),” Sen. Cantwell said prior to the vote in a speech on the Senate floor.
“But compensation on revenue sharing is probably the most important thing we could possibly enshrine in federal law today. This is (Congress) saying, for the first time, that an athlete gets a percentage of the media rights, the ticket sales, and the sponsorship.”
Among other provisions, the Protect College Sports Act would:
–Cap agent fees at 5%.
–Guarantee scholarships for 10 years after eligibility so athletes can finish pursuing their degrees.
–Mandate Division I schools cover out-of-pocket medical costs for sports- related injuries or illness for current student athletes for five years post- eligibility.
–Ban schools from pulling scholarships due to an injury or poor performance.
–Allow athletes to transfer once with immediate eligibility at the new school.
–Prevent football coaches from moving to a new school midseason.
–Require schools to maintain a minimum number of women’s and Olympic sports.
“We need to stop stealing money out of college (and) university institutions for education, for tuition, for professors, and putting it into an arms race on sports,” Cantwell said. “It is putting a pin in the problems to stabilize the loss of women’s and Olympic (sports) and to create the opportunity to discuss the larger structure moving forward. That is why I think we have so much support.”
Cruz said, “We are here, at long last, on the verge of something historic.”
In the lengthy Senate debate on Monday, among the amendments added to the bill was allowing power conferences to have up to 20 teams. The previous version set the cap at 19.
If the House passes the bill, it would need President Donald Trump’s signature to become law. Trump has expressed his support for the Protect College Sports Act.
(–Field Level Media)

sources.news_title: What Changes to Expect as U.S. Senate Passes Protect College Sports Act, NCAA President Releases Statement
sources.text:
Late Monday night, the U.S. Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act (PCSA) in a 77-22 vote. Led by Texas Republican Ted Cruz and Washington Democrat Maria Cantwell, this bill promises the biggest change in college sports history. But do not celebrate just yet! The bill now heads to the House of Representatives, where passage is far from guaranteed. Until the House passes it and the President signs it, none of these major changes actually go into effect.
Watch What’s Trending Now!
For years, the NCAA and major conferences have been begging Washington for a single national law to replace the patchwork of state rules. Now, as On3 reported, Senator Cruz summarized the high stakes on the Senate floor Monday: “This bill is about what makes college sports uniquely American.”
With this vote, college sports are officially closer than ever to having a unified, government-backed playbook. If this bill officially clears the House of Representatives and becomes law, it will completely freeze and regulate the frantic worlds of NIL money, athlete transfers, and conference expansion.
Even President Donald Trump is in favor of it.
“The Protect College Sport Act just passed in the U.S. Senate by a vote of 77-22,” he said about the bill. “This is a really big deal. It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves.”
Here’s the thing: Congress did not just pull these ideas out of thin air. For over a decade, court decisions like O’Bannon v. NCAA and the recent multi-billion-dollar House v. NCAA settlement slowly broke the NCAA’s old amateur rules. Lawmakers are now trying to take those court settlements and write them into federal law so colleges stop getting dragged into court every year.
It also adds a $22.5 million fund to help schools keep players and a $5 million fund for women and all other sorts of non-revenue sports. It also requires multimedia rights companies and third-party collectives to confirm that outside NIL deals are not being used as a hidden way to get around the $50 million cap.
The bill also puts a massive dent in the wild-west transfer portal that has left rosters feeling like temporary parking lots.
Under the PCSA, athletes are strictly allowed to transfer only once during their entire college career. The only real exceptions where players can jump ship a second time without penalty are in the event of a head coaching change, the total discontinuation of their sport, or documented university misconduct.
However, graduate transfers will still get an exception and can play right away. The bill also gives the NCAA more power to stop tampering and enforce transfer rules across states. It would also override the NIL laws already in place in some states.
In simple terms, college sports are trying to look like professional leagues without calling players employees. The NFL and NBA already use central rules, trade deadlines, and capped contracts, but they do it through union agreements. Since college athletes do not have a union, the Senate is trying to act like a referee and set those same rules from above.
But that’s not where it ends. There would be restrictions on coaches, too, via the ‘Lane Kiffin Rule’. This rule targets itchy coaching feet and strictly prevents any FBS head coach, coordinator, or assistant coach from completely abandoning their team for a new job in-season before the end of their current team’s schedule.
Additionally, the bill aims to slow down the constant conference realignment that has damaged historic rivalries. After summer changes made to gain support from the SEC and Big Ten, the PCSA would limit any conference making more than $700 million in revenue to a maximum of 20 members.
For the first six years of the law, any Power Four team that wants to leave its conference for another one would have to spend three years independent before joining a new conference. The bill would also protect schools from antitrust issues when they work together to sell their media rights.
While NCAA President Charlie Baker celebrated the vote, he made sure to remind everyone that the battle isn’t over yet.
Right after the vote, Baker stated that “the Senate’s passage of the Protect College Sports Act is a historic milestone for student-athletes and universities alike,” but quickly added that “there is still much work left to do to ensure this vital framework becomes law.”
Beyond these roster caps, the act would also improve player safety by creating independent NCAA compliance oversight on college campuses. This would set minimum standards for athlete healthcare and medical insurance, and guarantee 10-year scholarships so players can finish their degrees after their playing careers end.
The bill would also cap sports agent fees at 5% to help protect players from being overcharged.
Other changes…
Despite overwhelming bipartisan support, the bill has faced backlash from critics who argue it hurts player leverage. The Congressional Black Caucus and Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy fiercely opposed the legislation, arguing that it intentionally suppresses the earning potential of young athletes.
Opponents claim the law was designed to protect the billions of dollars pocketed by universities, wealthy coaches, and television executives, all while refusing to give the actual student-athletes a seat at the negotiating table.
Player advocates support regulation but argue rules should be negotiated with athletes, not imposed by lawmakers. Now, the Protect College Sports Act officially heads to the U.S. House of Representatives for a showdown.
The timeline is incredibly tight. Apparently, the House isn’t expected to return to Washington, D.C., until after the midterm elections in mid-November.
However, Senator Eric Schmitt, a co-author of the bill, told On3 on Monday, “I would like to do it sooner rather than later. The president is very committed to this and wants to get this thing done, too.”
Senator Ted Cruz has even publicly floated the idea that Trump should sign the bill live on a broadcast of ESPN’s College GameDay once it clears Congress to officially ring in a brand-new era of American sports.

sources.news_title: Trump calls College Sports Act ‘really big deal’ - but what changes?
sources.text:
President Donald Trump called the Protect College Sports Act a “really big deal” after the Senate passed the legislation 77-22 on Monday.
“This is a really big deal. It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
“Congratulations to Randy Levine, President of the New York Yankees, and all of those who worked with him, on a job well done!” he added.
The U.S. Senate passed the act in a push to reform the collegiate athletic system's protocol on transfers and player likeness payments.
The bill would establish rules governing college athletics as lawmakers seek to bring greater stability to a system reshaped by athletes’ ability to earn money from their name, image and likeness.
What College Sports Act Changes
The Protect College Sports Act would create national rules governing how college athletes are paid, how they can make money from their name, image and likeness (NIL), and when they can transfer between schools.
This would replace the current patchwork of NCAA rules, state laws and court decisions with a national framework, while incorporating elements of the House v. NCAA settlement, which allows schools to directly share revenue with their athletes.
The bill would set a limit on how much schools can directly pay athletes through revenue sharing, while creating new federal rules for NIL deals, including disclosure and contract requirements.
Athletes would generally be allowed one transfer without losing a year of eligibility, with a five-year limit on eligibility. It would also give the NCAA greater authority to enforce the rules, while providing additional protections for athletes' scholarships and medical coverage.
Bill Advances to House
The bipartisan bill was co-authored by Republican Senator Ted Cruz and Democratic Sentator Maria Cantwell.
The upper chamber's passage now advances the bill to the House of Representatives for a vote.
Supporters argue that congressional action is needed to replace an assortment of state laws while critics have raised concerns about limiting athletes’ rights.
Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat, took to X on Monday night to voice his opposition saying, "College athletes put their bodies on the line every day—and generate billions of dollars for their universities, conferences, and the NCAA. The Protect College Sports Act pulls the rug out from under them. I will keep fighting alongside college athletes until they get the rights and protections they deserve."
In an email sent to Newsweek following the vote, Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and chairman of the U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce, Science & Transportation said, "Today is a monumental day for college athletics. The United States Senate voted to protect the hundreds of thousands of student athletes currently competing in college sports, the millions who will follow in their footsteps, and every college sports fan who wants to preserve this great American tradition for generations to come."
"After years of discussions and months of intense deliberations, we achieved what many said was impossible and succeeded in getting the Protect College Sports Act through the Senate with a huge bipartisan vote. I am proud of our success, and I trust the House of Representatives will remain focused on bringing stability to college sports by delivering the Protect College Sports Act to President Trump’s desk without delay.”
The bill follows a 2025 court settlement that allowed schools to pay athletes for their image, likeness and name, the Associated Press reports.
Senators Who Voted Against the Bill

sources.news_title: Senate passes sweeping college sports bill to regulate athlete pay, transfers
sources.text:
The Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill on Monday that would regulate college sports, an attempt to end “chaos” in an industry that has been upended by skyrocketing athlete payments and near-unrestricted transfers between schools.
The overwhelming 77-22 vote to pass the legislation is the strongest effort yet by Congress to set national regulations governing payments to college athletes for their name, image and likeness and how often they can transfer. It would give the NCAA new authority over those rules and limited antitrust protections to enforce them.
The bill is the product of years of Senate negotiations that intensified after a 2025 lawsuit settlement uprooted the college sports landscape by allowing colleges to pay their players. The legislation, which would still have to pass the House, would codify the settlement into law but also establish new guardrails around the system in an attempt to rein in the runaway costs for colleges.
“It would be nice if college sports could somehow magically fix itself, but this is a matter of law, federal law, and only Congress can fix it,” said Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who negotiated the bill with the top Democrat on the panel, Washington Sen. Maria Cantwell.
President Donald Trump praised the bill in a social media post after the late night passage. “This is a really big deal,” he said. “It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves.”
The bill's backers — more than 70 senators from both parties — say it aims to curtail constant litigation and uncertainty across college sports for athletes, schools and fans. It would also give hundreds of thousands of athletes new health and labor protections.
But critics say the bill doesn't do enough to protect athletes or curtail the enormous sums of money flowing to coaches, colleges and conferences.
“This is a bill that essentially ensconces a system of exploitation, and it doesn’t fix the broader problems,” said Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy, a Democrat who has worked with labor and civil rights groups to rally opposition to the bill.
The bill’s future is still unclear. It could face an uphill battle in the House, which failed repeatedly over the last year to get a different version to the floor and is in recess until after the November elections.
Lawmakers will have to start over in the next Congress if the bill doesn't pass both chambers by the end of the year.
Bill addresses skyrocketing spending, unlimited transfers
College sports have been reeling in the wake of the 2025 court settlement allowing colleges to directly pay players for their name, image and likeness. The fallout has reshaped the industry and led to football roster payrolls that can exceed $40 million.
The bill would codify the court settlement, including a revenue cap that allows schools to share up to $21.5 million in revenue with their players. The legislation would more than double that amount for some schools, allowing up to an additional $27.5 million in payments through a retention fund — a change that helped win the support of the two largest conferences, the Big Ten and Southeastern Conference.
To help schools raise more revenue, the bill would give schools and conferences the option of pooling their TV media rights.
RELATED STORY | NCAA approves new eligibility rules giving Division I athletes 5 years to play 5 seasons
The legislation also aims to stabilize the NCAA transfer portal that has led to players constantly switching teams. It would restrict player transfers to one “free” move over five years without sitting out a year, with some exceptions, and also would restrict players to five years of total eligibility.
The proposed eligibility limit comes amid backlash to schools that have increasingly pushed boundaries, including LSU's now-canceled plans to place players on the roster who had participated in NFL training camps.
“That was probably like a big lamp for some people who saw it and said, ‘Oh my God, this is so out of control,’” Cantwell said in a recent interview with The Associated Press.
The bill also would restrict coaches from leaving their schools during the season, force schools that want to switch conferences to spend three years as an independent and prevent conferences from growing larger than 20 programs — an effort to prevent so-called “superleagues” from taking over sports. A last-minute amendment proposed by Florida Sen. Ashley Moody raised that cap from 19 in the original legislation.
The vote was delayed several hours on Monday as senators negotiated Moody’s amendment and others that were eventually adopted, including a provision to make it easier for athletes to sue over sexual assault and a requirement to disclose foreign financing.
The Senate rejected an amendment by Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., that would have put limits on ticket prices for fans and two by Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., that would have capped coaches’ salaries at $5 million a year and increased compensation for athletes who have catastrophic injuries.
Critics say it wouldn’t do enough to help athletes
The legislation includes new protections for athletes, including caps on agent fees and guarantees for health insurance and scholarships. It would also require schools to maintain a minimum number of sports and roster spots — an effort to ensure that women's and Olympic sports are not cut in favor of football, basketball and other sports that generate more revenue.
Still, some Democrats say it wouldn't do enough to limit the big money in college sports.
The legislation “places a cap on the students’ cut of the revenues, but there are no caps on coaches’ salaries or on the size of donations to athletic programs,” Murphy said last week.
Groups like the NAACP, Congressional Black Caucus and AFL-CIO have also opposed the bill, in part, because it leaves unresolved whether athletes should be considered employees with the ability to collectively bargain.
RELATED STORY | SEC sues LSU, alleging a coordinated push to recruit ex-pro athletes in defiance of rules
All four Black Democrats in the Senate — Booker, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland — have opposed the bill.
Booker, who played football at Stanford in the late 1980s on a scholarship, noted the “outsized role” that Black athletes play in college sports. He said it wasn't until college athletes were able to begin to win cases in court that the power started to shift, “and now the NCAA is coming here to the United States Senate, asking for sweeping powers" to exempt antitrust laws.
“We know who this bill is protecting,” Booker said.
House passage is uncertain
Despite strong bipartisan support in the Senate, the bill faces a murky path in the House.
House lawmakers won't return to Washington until mid-November, after the elections. And it's unclear what will be on Republican leaders' agenda in the chaotic last few weeks of the session.
Pressure from Trump could help push the bill to passage. But some House Republicans have insisted on language explicitly stating that athletes are not employees, which the Senate bill does not have — a key concession to Cantwell to win enough Democratic support.
After the bill's passage, Cruz said it is his hope “that we see in the House the same thing we saw in the Senate: a big bipartisan vote.”

sources.news_title: U.S. Senate passes Ted Cruz's college sports bill
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — After several months in limbo, U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz’s bill that would impose a sweeping set of regulations on college sports passed the Senate late Monday night with more than three quarters of the body’s support, marking the legislation’s furthest milestone yet.
Sponsored by Cruz, the Senate Commerce Committee chair, and Ranking Member Maria Cantwell, D-Washington, the Protect College Sports Act had remained stalled since it advanced through the committee in June. After hours of discussion Monday on amendments that saw minor changes to the bill, it finally passed in the upper chamber 77-22. The bill must still clear the U.S. House, which is in recess until after the November elections, before reaching the desk of President Donald Trump.
Cruz’s bill would install a slew of regulations to rectify what he frequently has called the “chaos” that’s emerged since the NCAA’s 2021 decision to allow college athletes to profit off their name, image and likeness, or NIL, and after a subsequent settlement a few years later, House v. NCAA, forced the association and its athletic conferences to share revenue with athletes. College athletics continue to operate under varying state laws, court rulings and NCAA regulations that govern everything from athlete compensation to conference realignment.
On the Senate floor Monday, Cruz said the bill “protects our student-athletes.”
“It protects NIL opportunities, because student-athletes deserve the opportunity to benefit from their talent without being taken advantage of by unscrupulous agents and backdoor deals,” Cruz said. “It creates clear, enforceable rules for eligibility and transfers. It protects our traditions and rivalries. It prevents the most powerful and wealthy conferences from breaking away to form a super league.”
The bill garnered fresh momentum at the start of August, when Cruz, other lawmakers and White House officials won the support of Big Ten and Southeastern Conference leaders, who got on board after Cruz and Cantwell revised the bill’s revenue sharing framework. Soon after, the White House formally voiced its support for the bill, with Trump calling on lawmakers to move quickly to pass it. Cruz has recently pressed the House to return to Capitol Hill to pass the legislation.
“What I would like to see is the speaker call the House back to pass this bill and put it on the president’s desk,” he said on his podcast last week, adding that he has “urged the president to sign it on the set of College Gameday, do it on a big game and do it going into the election.”
Among other provisions, the bill would enshrine some recent legal victories for athletes while also establishing stricter regulations on their activity. Schools and athletic organizations could no longer restrict athletes from entering NIL agreements, while athletes would have to report their revenue above $600 to their institutions. It would also limit athletes to one transfer throughout their college careers and establish permanent ceilings on their revenue, with annual adjustments for inflation.
The legislation also aims to protect athletic programs that don’t return huge profits. Division I conferences would be prohibited from reducing their schools’ required number of varsity or Olympic sports teams. Schools that make $80 million or more in annual athletics revenue would have to at least maintain 2024-25 levels of scholarships and roster spots for sports that don’t generate a profit.
For Ruben Rojas Betanzos, a Syracuse University student-athlete, president of Syracuse’s Student-Athlete Advisory Committee and vice chair of the Atlantic Coast Conference’s committee, the rapidly changing landscape has made it increasingly difficult for athletes to know what rules apply to them.
“Rules are changing so quickly that it’s almost impossible for someone to keep up,” Betanzos told The Texas Tribune. “A student-athlete in one state could be having a completely different experience from an athlete in another state.”
Betanzos, who is in his fifth year at Syracuse and completing a masters in business administration after studying bioengineering as an undergraduate, said he supports the bill’s provisions addressing healthcare, Olympic and women’s sports, and capping agent endorsement fees at 5%.
Other notable college sports figures have voiced their support for the legislation, like former University of Alabama football head coach Nick Saban and Deion Sanders, current head coach of the University of Colorado Boulder football team.
But the bill has drawn significant opposition from labor and civil rights organizations, as well as some lawmakers who argue that it would give the NCAA and athletic conferences too much control over athletes.
In an August letter to Senate leadership, NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson urged lawmakers to reject the legislation.
“Congress should not grant new federal benefits, legal protections, or economic advantages to public institutions and athletic conferences that profit from the talent and labor of Black college athletes while remaining silent as their states dilute Black voting power,” he wrote. “That arrangement is a modern version of Jim Crow.”
Black athletes make up about 20 percent of Division I athletes and more than 40 percent of Division I men’s basketball and football players, according to NCAA figures.
The AFL-CIO, a major federation of U.S. labor unions, also urged senators to oppose the bill in a letter signed by Jody Calemine, director of government affairs. The letter took aim at the legislation’s antitrust exemption for universities and conferences, and argued that the bill halts the progress that athletes have made in combating their exploitation through collusion.
“The bill only gained its current momentum not when athletes’ interests were satisfied but when the richest intercollegiate conferences in the country voted to endorse the bill,” the letter read. “That should tell you everything you need to know about who this bill protects.”
Gabby Birenbaum contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Legislators back effort to regulate college athletics | Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
sources.text:
WASHINGTON -- Both of Arkansas' U.S. senators voted Monday in favor of legislation regulating college athletics, an attempt to bring control to an era of player payments and transfers.
The Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act in a 77-22 vote, sending the bill to the House of Representatives for its consideration.
Sens. John Boozman and Tom Cotton, both Republicans, supported the measure throughout the legislative process. Boozman, who played football at the University of Arkansas, said Congress needs to put college sports "under better control" as athletes make money from their name, image and likeness.
"Really, the absence of the NCAA enforcing the rules has created a huge problem," the Rogers senator said.
The Protect College Sports Act is a response to a June 2025 court settlement allowing institutions to pay players directly. The settlement also led to the creation of the College Sports Commission, an independent body responsible for enforcing the agreement's terms on revenue sharing; name, image and likeness; and roster limits.
The current revenue sharing cap allows institutions to share $21.5 million in revenue with players, but critics say the commission has been unsuccessful in enforcing the settlement's terms, pointing to college football programs with rosters worth more than $40 million.
The Protect College Sports Act would codify the settlement's terms. The bill would also allow colleges to establish a $22.5 million fund for retaining students who have spent less than a season at the institution. Colleges and conferences could also pool and sell certain media rights to generate revenue.
Under the bill, players would have five years to play college sports, and they could transfer once without losing their eligibility. The measure also aims to stop coaches from leaving their jobs during the season, although senators rejected an amendment with further restrictions on coaches, including a $5 million salary cap.
The original legislation would have prevented conferences from having more than 19 members -- an attempt to prevent the largest conferences from forming a "super league" -- but senators approved an amendment increasing the cap to 20 institutions.
Senators inserted language in the measure to protect Olympic and women's sports programs, fearing colleges could cut these teams to support revenue-generating programs and address mounting debt. Colleges could establish a $5 million fund for supporting "non-revenue generating" programs, and certain midsized and large institutions would need to maintain roster spots and scholarships for these athletes.
"If we continue the way we are going, we're essentially going to have a lot of schools with football and basketball teams," Boozman told the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette. "We'll lose a lot of the sports that aren't generating revenue."
Cotton, of Little Rock, cited the future of Olympic and women's sports as a reason for supporting the legislation.
"As I've traveled around the state, many Arkansans have expressed concern that the current path college sports are heading down would only serve the biggest programs and would leave behind everyone else, including Olympic and women's sports," the senator said in a statement. "The Protect College Sports Act would institute a national rulebook that provides consistency and fairness to Arkansas universities, student athletes, and fans."
Several college athletic conferences back the bill, including the Southeastern Conference and the Sun Belt Conference. During its Sept. 17 meeting, the University of Arkansas System Board of Trustees approved a resolution expressing support for the Protect College Sports Act.
The Trump administration also endorsed the Senate effort. The White House issued a statement of administration policy in August describing the legislation as a "crucial step toward bicameral legislation that will preserve and strengthen" college sports.
Boozman acknowledged John Calipari, the University of Arkansas men's basketball coach, as a significant force behind the bill's success so far. Calipari traveled to Capitol Hill earlier this month to urge senators to pass the legislation.
"He's been up here constantly," the senator noted.
Calipari was not available for an interview regarding the measure. In a Sept. 17 social media video, the coach said the bill could "calm the waters" of college sports.
"It'll bring together all of us and give us some stability," he said. "The bill is not perfect, but I believe this solves 75% to 80% of our issues, and it's really been special to see both parties come together and work toward a solution."
The NAACP and the Congressional Black Caucus oppose the measure, arguing Congress should not pursue legislation regulating college sports as several states make decisions the organizations say will restrict Black voting rights. Both groups have directed their criticisms toward Republican-led states that have approved new congressional maps at President Donald Trump's behest.
"When their revenues, competitive positions, or legal exposure are at issue, these institutions have no difficulty finding their voices," NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson wrote in an Aug. 4 letter to Senate leaders.
"Yet, when Black communities ask those same institutions to oppose racially discriminatory maps and the dilution of Black voting strength, too many retreat behind claims of institutional neutrality," he continued. "Silence under those circumstances is not neutrality. It is a decision to devalue Black participation while profiting from Black talent."
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., has been critical of the bill for not doing enough to address the "runaway costs" of college sports, noting how much institutions spend on facilities and coaching salaries.
During a Monday floor speech, Murphy drew specific attention to Louisiana State University. The institution's athletic program is projecting a $26 million deficit for the current fiscal year and has overspent its budget by $177.5 million over the past six years.
"But LSU just agreed to pay their new (football) coach Lane Kiffin $91 million over seven years along with other bonuses to him," Murphy said on the Senate floor, adding the institution also owes $54 million to former football head coach Brian Kelly after firing him last year.
"If you want to know what's driving the deficit at these big schools, it's not simply the amount of money they are paying the students," the senator said.
The House has its own bill addressing college sports, but the chamber has not considered this measure. House members will remain away from Capitol Hill until after the midterm elections in November, when lawmakers will face limited time to complete an already packed legislative agenda.

The U.S. Senate approved a landmark federal framework for college sports Monday, voting 72-22 to bring order to a multibillion-dollar industry whose biggest events can draw television audiences comparable to major professional championships.
The bipartisan Protect College Sports Act would regulate how universities pay athletes, restrict transfers and give the governing NCAA limited protection from antitrust lawsuits after years of court battles transformed the economics of college athletics.
The vote was one of the Senate’s last major legislative acts before lawmakers leave Washington to campaign for the November 3 midterm elections.
The bill now goes to the House of Representatives, which is already in recess until after Election Day, leaving a narrow window for Congress to complete work before a new legislature takes office in January.
President Donald Trump’s administration has endorsed the legislation, and the 80-year-old leader himself cheered the bill’s passage Monday night, posting to his Truth Social platform that “it will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves.”
Unlike university sports in most countries, American college athletics is a vast commercial enterprise.
More than 30 million people watched January’s college football national championship on TV while the major conferences — regional groupings of universities that organize competition and negotiate media rights — have signed multibillion-dollar broadcasting contracts.
The legislation follows years of upheaval during which athletes won the right to profit from their names and images and, following a 2025 court settlement, universities began paying players directly.
It would establish national rules governing those payments and allow schools to spend nearly $50 million annually through revenue-sharing and other funds.
Athletes would generally be allowed one transfer without sitting out a season, while agents’ fees would be capped at five percent.
The bill also provides longer-term scholarship and healthcare protections and seeks to safeguard women’s and Olympic sports.
Supporters argue that nationwide rules are needed to replace a patchwork of state laws and repeated litigation.
“Student athletes deserve to get paid. They deserve real protections. And high school athletes deserve a fair shot to compete,” said Senator Ted Cruz, who co-sponsored the bill.
“The Protect College Sports Act delivers that while protecting women’s and Olympic sports and preserving the game we love for generations to come,” the Texas Republican added.

sources.news_title: Delaware's lawmakers split as Protect College Sports Act passes Senate
sources.text:
The Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill on Monday that would regulate college sports, an attempt to end “chaos” in an industry that has been upended by skyrocketing athlete payments and near-unrestricted transfers between schools.
The overwhelming 77-22 vote to pass the legislation is the strongest effort yet by Congress to set national regulations governing payments to college athletes for their name, image and likeness and how often they can transfer. It would give the NCAA new authority over those rules and limited antitrust protections to enforce them.
The bipartisan support of the bill did not extend to Delaware, where the two Democrats took opposite stances.
Lisa Blunt Rochester voted against the bill, while Chris Coons, an original co-sponsor of the bill, supported it on the Senate floor, and spoke about it afterwards.
“College sports are in crisis, and I’m grateful to Senators Cantwell and Cruz for leading this bipartisan effort to save them. Their hard work negotiating with colleges and universities, HBCUs, the NCAA, unions, trial lawyers, players, and others has created a badly needed bill that is a win for student-athletes, schools, and fans. Today’s resounding, bipartisan vote for final passage that won the support of a majority of my Democratic colleagues is proof of their success.
“No matter which school they attend or what sport they play, this bill will protect the education, health, and compensation rights of all 550,000 NCAA student-athletes. It keeps college sports from collapsing and leaves student-athletes better off than before. I want to thank my colleagues for taking up and passing this bill so swiftly, and I urge the House to do the same,” Coons said.
The bill is the product of years of Senate negotiations that intensified after a 2025 lawsuit settlement uprooted the college sports landscape by allowing colleges to pay their players. The legislation, which would still have to pass the House, would codify the settlement into law but also establish new guardrails around the system in an attempt to rein in the runaway costs for colleges.
“It would be nice if college sports could somehow magically fix itself, but this is a matter of law, federal law, and only Congress can fix it,” said Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who negotiated the bill with the top Democrat on the panel, Washington Sen. Maria Cantwell.
The bill’s backers — more than 70 senators from both parties — say it aims to curtail constant litigation and uncertainty across college sports for athletes, schools and fans. It would also give hundreds of thousands of student athletes new health and labor protections.
But critics say the bill doesn’t do enough to protect athletes or curtail the enormous sums of money flowing to coaches, colleges and conferences.
“This is a bill that essentially ensconces a system of exploitation, and it doesn’t fix the broader problems,” said Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy, a Democrat who has worked with labor and civil rights groups to rally opposition to the bill.
The bill’s future is still unclear.
UPDATE | Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester issued a statement about her "no" vote, which was supported by the Congressional Black Caucus:
“The landscape of college sports is changing by the day, and Congress undoubtedly has a responsibility to come together to find a path forward. However, while I appreciate the bipartisan work put into this bill, I remain concerned with it — especially in this moment.
“Despite the bill providing a private right of action for student-athletes, it relies on individual athletes to enforce their rights through litigation. Student-athletes often have limited time, resources, and legal expertise. They should not bear primary responsibility for identifying violations and suing their schools or athletic programs to secure the protections provided by the bill.
“I am also concerned that the bill would codify significant terms governing student-athletes’ compensation, transfers, and eligibility at a time when questions about athletes’ labor rights remain unsettled. Congress should not lock these terms into federal law in ways that could limit student-athletes’ ability to negotiate or collectively bargain over them in the future.
“The adequacy of athlete protections has raised concerns for student-athletes, their families, civil rights organizations, labor organizations, and other athlete advocates, and should be fully considered as the legislation moves forward. I’m hopeful that Congress can come back together to find a solution that is fair and comprehensive for both universities and the students they serve.”
WDEL's Sean Greene contributed to this article
